title: Chamier: faith is voluntary intellect-act commanded by will (Thomas)
source_text: IX. Sed praesertim multus est super ea re Daniel Chamierus, Panstratiae Tom. 3. lib. 12. cap. 4. de Fide, paragr. 6. & sequentibus. Ubi multis argumentis probat fidem esse voluntariam, id est, a voluntate ortum suum habere, & esse actum intellectus a voluntate imperatum; alios enim actus intellectus a voluntate pendere, alios vero non pendere, fidem vero esse de priorum numero; adeoque quemadmodum omnia bona opera sunt a voluntate nostra, tanquam a causa, ita etiam fidem ab eadem nostra voluntate ut a causa secunda esse. Itaque tanquam suum adoptat illud Thomae, Credere ad intellectum pertinet, prout est a voluntate motus ad assentiendum. Cujus rei hanc rationem affert par. 13. Nempe quod motus quo fertur intellectus ad verum, & qui dicitur assensus, fit dupliciter. Alias, per rationem, id est, evidentiam rei; quomodo in scientiis plerisque conclusiones persuadentur ex vi principiorum. Et hic assensus necessarius est, nempe quia quodammodo cogitur animus vi rationum. Alias, is motus fit a voluntate, nimirum, quum res est obscura, id est, remotior a captu mentis humanae, quae tum cogitur quasi palpare in tenebris, luce illa rationum destituta. Itaque, quomodo in tenebris non potest oculus objectum apprehendere, propter subtractionem lucis intermediae, ita intellectus obscuras res non potest percipere, deficiente rationum lumine. Proinde tum voluntatis partes esse necesse est, haec enim intellectum movet ad assensum rei alioquin incognitae. Jam in Theologia quis nescit non esse rationum evidentiam. Oportet ergo in Theologia, vel assensum nullum esse, vel esse a voluntate movente intellectum. Hactenus Chamierus.
pass_a_gloss: But Daniel Chamier is especially full on this matter in Panstratia tom. 3 book 12 ch. 4 on Faith, §§6ff. There with many arguments he proves faith is voluntary — that is, has its origin from the will, and is an act of intellect commanded by the will; for some intellect-acts depend on the will and others do not, and faith is of the former number; and just as all good works are from our will as from a cause, so also faith is from that same will as from a secondary cause. And so he adopts as his own that saying of Thomas: To believe belongs to the intellect insofar as it is moved by the will to assent. The reason (§13): the motion by which intellect is carried to the true, called assent, happens in two ways. Sometimes by reason, that is, evidence of the thing — as in most sciences conclusions are persuaded by force of principles — and this assent is necessary because the mind is somehow compelled by reasons. Sometimes the motion is from the will, namely when the thing is obscure, farther from human grasp, so that the mind must as it were grope in darkness without that light of reasons. As the eye cannot seize an object in darkness when intermediate light is withdrawn, so intellect cannot perceive obscure things when the light of reasons fails. Then the will's part is necessary: it moves intellect to assent to what is otherwise unknown. And who does not know there is no evidence of reasons in Theology? Therefore in Theology either there is no assent, or it is from the will moving the intellect. Thus far Chamier.
pass_b_english: Chamier (Panstratia 3.12.4): faith is a will-commanded intellect act (with Thomas).
Science assents by evidence; theology's obscure truths need the will to move assent — else no assent at all.

choices.why: Origin from will as secondary cause, not bare whim.
